title: Load harness variance forensics & priming notes
content:
Purpose:
This note collects a pragmatic forensic checklist and experimental matrix for investigating run-to-run throughput variance in the serving runtime. Focus is on: short-lived spikes/dips in tokens/sec, irreproducible throughput regressions after code or config changes, and failures to reach expected steady-state throughput.

Scope and motivation:
- Not a new benchmark spec; complements existing harnesses by prescribing a stepwise diagnostic flow and concrete configs to isolate causes (warmup artifacts, RNG/caching, batching, OS noise, power/thermal throttling, driver differences).
- Intended audience: perf engineers, SREs running baseline regression triage, and oncall owners who need fast root-cause heuristics.

Observed symptoms (examples seen on infra):
- nominal tokens/sec changes 3–12% between runs with identical load inputs
- long-tailed p95 latency increases intermittently while median remains stable
- throughput slowly ramps and never stabilizes even after expected warmup period
- repeatable regressions only on specific hosts or GPU drivers

High-level hypotheses to test (quick triage order):
1) Priming / KV cache mismatch: different cache hit rates cause apparent run differences
2) RNG/seed differences in synthetic load causing different length/occupancy distributions
3) Batching heat/cold effects: batch formation latency due to client pacing jitter
4) System noise: background processes, CPU governor, power caps, thermal throttling
5) Driver/runtime mismatch: CUDA/driver/NCCL version interactions or kernel selection differences
6) Load harness issues: client-side concurrency, unintended retries, clock skew

Minimal reproducibility checklist (always run before blaming runtime):
- record git commit for serving-runtime, compiler flags, model artifact checksum (sha256), and model config (context length, dtype, quantization)
- capture nvidia-smi -q, nsys system profile, and dmesg before and after run
- freeze host configuration: CPU governor = performance, THP disabled, disable power-save on NICs, pin loadgen process to dedicated CPU cores
- set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=0 (unless blocking used intentionally)
- ensure no other workloads on the GPU (nvidia-smi pids) and MIG profiles stable
- capture the exact loadgen command line and seed values

Instrumentation to enable (low-overhead first):
- loadgen-level: tokens/sec, qps, batch size histogram, client-side request timestamps (send/receive), request latencies (network / server observed), worker queue lengths
- runtime-level: batch formation latency histogram, kernel time breakdown, KV cache hit rate, sequence-length occupancy, active batch utilization % (GPU compute vs wait)
- system-level: GPU utilization, memory headroom, PCIe throughput, CPU steal, interrupts/sec, nvlink usage if applicable

Suggested experiments (matrix):
A) Seed hygiene: run identical RNG seed across loadgen runs and compare. If variance collapses, track down RNG sources (client shuffling, sampling).
B) Cache probe: run three variants — cold (clear cache between requests), warm (single priming pass), and controlled priming (repeat a small representative corpus 3x) — look at throughput and hit-rate curves.
C) Deterministic microbench: single-request tight loop on same model+host measuring kernel timings to exclude scheduler noise.
D) Driver swap: repeat short runs on alternative CUDA/driver minor revision (same major) to check kernel selection changes.
E) Occupancy stress: vary sequence-length mix (short/long), and observe batch packing efficiency and tail latency; helpful to include a synthetic distribution file.
F) OS-noise stress: run with tuned vs default CPU governors, and with background I/O/cron jobs intentionally enabled to replicate observed noise.

Warmup and priming strategies (practical notes):
- Distribution-aware priming: prime with a corpus that matches the operational sequence-length distribution rather than simple repeated prompt. This prevents misleading batch formation behavior when live traffic is long-tailed.
- Two-phase warmup: fast initial primer (10–20% of target concurrency for 30–60s) followed by full-concurrency annealing for 2–5 minutes. Record curves to establish stabilization time.
- Controlled KV-cache seeding: when serving decoder-only models, seed the model with a small measurable set of prefixes and then measure hit-rate and performance; include a version with explicit KV-cache flush between iterations.
- Adaptive warmup heuristic: stop warmup when moving-window throughput variance < threshold for N consecutive windows (example threshold: 2% over 30s windows). Useful in automated CI runs to shorten unnecessary warmup.

Concrete loadgen snippets (conceptual, adapt to our harness):
- example: ./loadgen --target-concurrency 64 --qps 0 --seed 1234 --input-corpus dist.json --duration 300 --trace-points batch_formation,kvcache_hit
- use --qps 0 to let concurrency drive batching; use a fixed seed and an explicit corpus file to avoid online shuffling differences

Metrics to capture and compare (baseline set):
- steady-state tokens/sec (mean + std), median and p50/p95/p99 latencies, batch_size distribution, batch_fill_factor (avg active tokens / token capacity), kv_cache_hit_rate, kernel_time_pct (time spent in kernels vs batching overhead), GPU_utilization_mean, CPU_steal_pct

Post-run statistical checks:
- sanity thresholds: if runs differ by <1–2% and within noise envelope, treat as equivalent for release gating
- use bootstrap sampling of per-request tokens/sec to produce 95% CI for throughput
- compute autocorrelation on throughput time series to detect persistent drift vs independent noise

Common root causes we found and quick mitigations:  
- asymmetric priming: one run used a longer priming set -> normalize priming.  
- hidden retries in client: enable request_id logging to detect duplicate requests.  
- thermal/perf state changes: pin CPU governor and capture powercap logs.  
- missing model quantization flags across nodes: add model artifact checksum validation to CI.  
- non-deterministic kernel selection: force deterministic kernel path via runtime flag when comparing changes.

Runbook (step-by-step triage):
1) Reproduce minimal failing pattern with short runs (2–5 min) and full instrumentation enabled.  
2) Confirm environment parity: git, model checksum, driver versions.  
3) Run seed-hygiene test (A) and cache probe (B).  
4) If difference persists, run microbench (C) on same host to separate scheduler noise vs runtime change.  
5) Swap driver/kernel (D) if microbench points to kernel variance.  
6) If still unclear, escalate with captured artifacts (nsys trace, perf counters, loadgen logs) to kernel/runtime owners.

Artifacts to attach to bug reports:
- nsys timeline (.qdrep), loadgen csv with per-request timestamps, model artifact sha256, serving-runtime logs (with nvtx markers), nvidia-smi -q output, kernel dmesg, and host perf counters.

Open TODOs and experiments planned:
- Automate adaptive warmup stop condition in CI harness (metric: 30s window var < 2%)
- Create small canonical corpus generator that can produce stable long-tail distributions for deterministic priming
- Add explicit kernel-selection logging in runtime to make driver-induced changes traceable from logs

Notes to self / scratch:
- when we witnessed 8% jitter last month, root cause ended up being intermittent background backups on a single host hitting NVMe bandwidth (look up ticket INF-1989)
- useful quick command: python -c 'import hashlib;print(hashlib.sha256(open("model.bin","rb").read()).hexdigest())' to verify model file consistency

Appendix: quick checklist to paste into CI job (shell):
- export SERVING_COMMIT=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
- sha256sum model.bin > model.sha256
- sudo cpupower frequency-set -g performance || echo 'no cpupower'
- sudo bash -c 'echo 0 > /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled' || true
- nvidia-smi -q > run-${SERVING_COMMIT}-nvidia.txt
- ./loadgen --seed 42 --input-corpus stable-corpus.json --duration 180 --trace=metrics.csv

End of note.
